era: The Reformations and their aftermath, 1517 to 1800

nodes.name: Moravian Church
nodes.summary: The Unity of Brethren arose from Bohemian reform before Luther. Refugees renewed its church life at Herrnhut in the eighteenth century.
nodes.why: Moravians carried earlier Czech reform into Protestant missions and influenced Wesley's search for assurance of faith.
facts: The Unity of Brethren organized at Kunwald in 1457.
Its founders drew on the reform associated with Jan Hus.
Zinzendorf welcomed Moravian refugees at Herrnhut in 1722.
Missionaries went to the Caribbean in 1732.
nodes.sacraments: Two: baptism, including infants, and Holy Communion. Moravians affirm Christ's presence and covenant fellowship without defining precisely how Christ is present in the elements.
nodes.today: Over one million worldwide, mainly eastern Africa, the Caribbean, and the Americas.
nodes.disputed: The church began in 1457. Its 1727 renewal continued that church rather than creating a Lutheran offshoot.

nodes.name: Luther's 95 Theses
nodes.summary: Martin Luther challenged indulgence preaching at Wittenberg in 1517. The dispute widened into separation from Rome by 1521.
nodes.why: Luther's challenge to indulgences began the dispute that led to Lutheran churches, although he initially sought reform within Catholicism.
facts: Luther circulated his theses on October 31, 1517.
Printing spread the controversy across Europe.
Pope Leo X excommunicated Luther in January 1521.
nodes.sacraments: The initial dispute concerned indulgences, repentance, and penance. Luther later challenged the Catholic sacramental system.
nodes.disputed: Posting the theses on the church door remains debated. Catholics and Lutherans interpret the later rupture differently.

nodes.name: Lutheran
nodes.summary: Luther and his colleagues built churches around justification by faith, biblical preaching, and sacraments as gifts of grace.
nodes.why: Lutheran churches teach that sacraments convey grace and Christ's body and blood are truly present in Communion.
facts: Luther initially worked as a Catholic monk and teacher.
The Augsburg Confession became a shared doctrinal standard.
The Book of Concord gathered Lutheran confessions in 1580.
nodes.sacraments: Usually two: baptism, including infants, and Eucharist. Both convey grace. Christ's body and blood are present with bread and wine in sacramental union. Absolution also has sacramental status.
nodes.today: Over 78 million in Lutheran World Federation churches, with others outside it.

nodes.name: Reformed
nodes.summary: Zwingli led reform in Zurich. Calvin later shaped Geneva. Their churches developed into Swiss, Dutch, French, Presbyterian, and related Reformed traditions.
nodes.why: Reformed churches form a major Protestant family with Communion teachings that differ from Lutheran sacramental union.
facts: Zwingli began preaching at Zurich's Grossmunster in 1519.
Zurich adopted reforms through public debates and council decisions.
Calvin and Bullinger agreed on Communion teaching in 1549.
Presbyterian churches belong to this wider family.
nodes.sacraments: Two: baptism, usually including infants, and the Lord's Supper. Calvin taught real spiritual presence and feeding through faith. Zwingli emphasized remembrance and rejected bodily presence.
nodes.today: About 100 million in World Communion of Reformed Churches member churches.

nodes.name: Diet of Worms
nodes.summary: Luther refused to retract his writings before Emperor Charles V. The Edict of Worms outlawed him and condemned his teachings.
nodes.why: Luther's survival depended on rulers willing to protect him against imperial law.
facts: Luther appeared before the diet in April 1521.
Charles V issued the edict in May.
Frederick the Wise sheltered Luther at Wartburg Castle.

nodes.name: Anabaptist
nodes.summary: Zurich reformers baptized professing believers rather than infants in 1525. Related movements elsewhere formed voluntary churches separate from state control.
nodes.why: Anabaptists made professed faith the basis for baptism and church membership. Mennonites, Hutterites, and Amish share these roots.
facts: Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock in Zurich on January 21, 1525.
Menno Simons gave Mennonites their name.
Hutterites began communal sharing in Moravia in 1528.
Jakob Ammann's followers separated in 1693, forming the Amish.
nodes.sacraments: Usually two ordinances or signs: believers' baptism and the Lord's Supper, remembering Christ and renewing community commitment. Many also practice footwashing.
nodes.today: About 2.13 million baptized believers worldwide, especially Africa, Asia, and the Americas.
nodes.disputed: The Zurich link records Swiss origins. Anabaptism also developed through distinct South German, Austrian, and Dutch movements.

nodes.name: Schleitheim Confession
nodes.summary: Swiss Brethren adopted seven articles at Schleitheim, defining baptism, discipline, Communion, church separation, leadership, nonviolence, and refusal of oaths.
nodes.why: The Swiss Brethren tied baptism to voluntary church membership and rejected violence, separating church life from political power.
facts: The gathering met on February 24, 1527.
Michael Sattler helped draft the articles.
The seven articles are not seven sacraments.
These articles did not represent every Anabaptist group.
nodes.sacraments: Baptism follows repentance and confessed faith. The Lord's Supper belongs to the baptized community committed to shared discipline.

nodes.name: Marburg Colloquy
nodes.summary: Luther and Zwingli agreed on many doctrines but could not agree about Christ's bodily presence in the Eucharist, blocking Protestant union.
nodes.why: Disagreement about Christ's presence in Communion prevented Luther and Zwingli from uniting their churches.
facts: Philip of Hesse convened the meeting in October 1529.
Luther defended Christ's bodily presence with bread and wine.
Zwingli interpreted the bread and wine as commemorative signs.
nodes.sacraments: Luther affirmed Christ's real bodily presence with bread and wine. Zwingli emphasized remembrance and rejected bodily presence in the elements.
nodes.disputed: Swiss reform began independently before Marburg. This split records failed union rather than descent from Lutheranism.

nodes.name: Augsburg Confession
nodes.summary: Philipp Melanchthon drafted a statement of Lutheran faith that Protestant rulers presented to Charles V at Augsburg.
nodes.why: Lutheran churches share this statement of belief about salvation, church life, baptism, and Communion.
facts: Representatives presented the confession on June 25, 1530.
It defended justification by faith.
It affirmed infant baptism and Christ's presence in Communion.

nodes.name: Act of Supremacy
nodes.summary: Parliament declared Henry VIII supreme head of the Church of England, replacing papal authority within England.
nodes.why: England broke with papal authority before its church adopted Protestant changes to worship and teaching.
facts: Henry sought annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon.
Parliament strengthened royal control through several acts.
Henry retained much Catholic doctrine and sacramental practice.
nodes.disputed: Anglicans claim continuity with England's ancient church. Catholics see the rejection of papal authority as schism.

nodes.name: Anglican
nodes.summary: England's church broke with papal authority, adopted Protestant reforms, and retained bishops and ordered worship. Related churches later formed a worldwide communion.
nodes.why: Anglican churches, including the American Episcopal Church, combine Reformed and Catholic sacramental emphases.
facts: Thomas Cranmer helped shape English worship and doctrine.
The Book of Common Prayer first appeared in 1549.
The 1563 Thirty-nine Articles express Reformation teaching.
nodes.sacraments: Two gospel sacraments: baptism, including infants, and Eucharist. Five other rites are commonly called sacraments. Communion teaching varies, including Reformed spiritual presence and Anglo-Catholic real presence.
nodes.today: About 85 million worldwide, especially Africa, Britain, and Commonwealth countries.

nodes.name: John Calvin
nodes.summary: John Calvin published the Institutes in 1536 and helped organize Geneva's Reformed church, returning in 1541 after exile.
nodes.why: Calvin's teaching shaped Reformed beliefs about grace, church discipline, and spiritual communion with Christ.
facts: Calvin expanded the Institutes through several editions, ending in 1559.
Calvin taught predestination and justification by faith.
Geneva trained ministers and sheltered Protestant refugees.
Calvin affirmed real spiritual feeding on Christ in Communion.

nodes.name: Menno Simons
nodes.summary: Menno Simons left the Catholic priesthood in 1536 and led Dutch Anabaptists committed to discipleship, believers' baptism, and nonviolence.
nodes.why: Mennonites take their name from a leader who helped nonviolent Anabaptist communities survive persecution.
facts: Menno served as a priest in Friesland.
His followers became known as Mennonites.
He rejected the violence associated with the Munster rebellion.

nodes.name: Jesuit Approval
nodes.summary: Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola and companions for preaching, education, and missions.
nodes.why: Jesuit schools and missions became part of Catholic renewal during the Protestant Reformations.
facts: Papal approval came on September 27, 1540.
Jesuits opened schools and served overseas missions.
The order remained within the Catholic Church.

nodes.name: Council of Trent
nodes.summary: Catholic bishops answered Protestant challenges, defined disputed teachings, and ordered reforms in clergy training and church discipline.
nodes.why: Trent defined Catholic sacramental teaching in response to Protestant challenges, preserving differences that still divide churches.
facts: The council met in several sessions between 1545 and 1563.
It reaffirmed seven sacraments in 1547.
It reaffirmed transubstantiation and Christ's real presence in 1551.
It required seminaries to improve priestly formation.
nodes.sacraments: Seven sacraments convey grace. Baptism includes infants. The Eucharist becomes Christ's body and blood through transubstantiation, while appearances of bread and wine remain.

nodes.name: Prayer Book and Articles
nodes.summary: The Book of Common Prayer introduced English worship services in 1549. The Thirty-nine Articles of 1563 set out the church's Reformation teaching.
nodes.why: Anglican worship and sacramental teaching draw on both the prayer book and the Articles.
facts: Thomas Cranmer led work on the first prayer book.
A more strongly Protestant revision appeared in 1552.
The Articles distinguish two gospel sacraments from five other rites.
The Articles reject transubstantiation and affirm spiritual reception of Christ.

nodes.name: Peace of Augsburg
nodes.summary: The Holy Roman Empire recognized Catholic and Lutheran territorial churches. Rulers generally determined their territories' religion, with provisions for dissenters to emigrate.
nodes.why: Rulers' religious choices helped turn reform movements into established regional churches.
facts: The agreement took effect on September 25, 1555.
It recognized churches adhering to the Augsburg Confession.
Reformed Christians and Anabaptists lacked recognition under this settlement.

nodes.name: Elizabethan Settlement
nodes.summary: Elizabeth I restored royal supremacy and Protestant worship after Mary I's Catholic restoration, using a revised prayer book and retaining bishops.
nodes.why: Elizabeth's settlement shaped the Church of England and left some reformers dissatisfied, contributing to Puritan dissent.
facts: The monarch became supreme governor rather than supreme head.
The Act of Uniformity required the 1559 prayer book.
Catholics and some Protestant reformers resisted the settlement.

nodes.name: Scottish Reformation
nodes.summary: John Knox and fellow reformers helped Scotland's Parliament adopt the Scots Confession and reject papal jurisdiction and the Mass.
nodes.why: Scotland's Reformed churches developed Presbyterian government, giving elders authority instead of bishops.
facts: Knox learned from Calvin during exile in Geneva.
Six ministers prepared the Scots Confession in 1560.
The First Book of Discipline proposed church and educational reforms.
Presbyterian government developed further over the following decades.

nodes.name: Congregationalist
nodes.summary: English Separatists and Puritans developed churches governed by their own congregations, drawing on Reformed beliefs while resisting control by bishops.
nodes.why: Congregationalists gave each local church authority over its own affairs. English Baptists emerged partly from these churches.
facts: Robert Browne organized a separatist congregation around 1581.
Some Puritans sought reform within England's church. Others separated.
Pilgrims brought congregational church life to Plymouth in 1620.
The Savoy Declaration of 1658 adapted Westminster teaching.
nodes.sacraments: Two sacraments or ordinances: baptism and the Lord's Supper. Historically, churches baptized infants and taught Christ's spiritual presence. Modern congregations vary, including memorial interpretations.
nodes.today: Millions worldwide, including united churches, especially Americas, Britain, southern Africa, and Pacific.
nodes.disputed: The Anglican link records English origins. The Reformed link records theology rather than a single formal church split.

nodes.name: Union of Brest
nodes.summary: Several bishops of the Kyivan metropolitan church entered communion with Rome while preserving Byzantine worship. Other bishops, clergy, and laypeople opposed the union.
nodes.why: Eastern Catholic churches can preserve Eastern worship while accepting communion with Rome.
facts: The union occurred in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
It contributed to today's Ukrainian and Belarusian Greek Catholic churches.
Orthodox communities continued outside the union.
Eastern Catholic churches also arose through other unions.
nodes.disputed: Catholic supporters describe restored communion. Orthodox opponents describe a divisive union accompanied by political pressure.

nodes.name: Baptist
nodes.summary: John Smyth and Thomas Helwys formed an English believers' baptism church in Amsterdam in 1609, emerging from Separatist and Puritan roots.
nodes.why: Baptists emerged from English Separatism. They share believers' baptism with Anabaptists without sharing a single origin.
facts: Dutch Mennonites influenced Smyth. Helwys resisted joining them.
Helwys established an English congregation around 1612 and defended religious liberty.
General Baptists taught that Christ died for all.
Particular Baptists emerged separately in the 1630s with Calvinist beliefs.
nodes.sacraments: Two ordinances: believers' baptism, usually immersion, and the Lord's Supper, usually memorial. Some Reformed Baptists also emphasize spiritual feeding on Christ.
nodes.today: At least 53 million baptized believers in Baptist World Alliance member churches.
nodes.disputed: Most historians trace Baptist origins to English Separatists. Some Baptists claim continuity with earlier churches rather than a seventeenth-century beginning.

nodes.name: Synod of Dort
nodes.summary: Dutch and international Reformed delegates rejected Remonstrant teachings and issued canons on election, atonement, human corruption, grace, and perseverance.
nodes.why: Calvinists and Arminians disagree about how God's grace relates to human response. Dort established the Reformed position.
facts: Delegates met at Dordrecht in the Netherlands.
The Remonstrants followed Jacob Arminius's challenge to Reformed teaching.
The Canons address five disputed points, not all Christian doctrine.
nodes.disputed: Reformed churches accepted the Canons as faithful teaching. Remonstrants rejected the verdict and faced political suppression.

nodes.name: Thirty Years' War
nodes.summary: War devastated central Europe as religious conflict intertwined with dynastic power. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secured recognition for Reformed churches.
nodes.why: Religious divisions and rulers' ambitions fueled devastating war. The peace recognized three confessions but stopped short of universal religious freedom.
facts: Fighting began with rebellion in Bohemia in 1618.
Catholic France opposed Catholic Habsburg rulers for political reasons.
Westphalia recognized Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed confessions in the Empire.
The settlement did not grant universal religious freedom.

nodes.name: Westminster Confession
nodes.summary: The Westminster Assembly completed a Reformed confession during the English Civil War. Scotland adopted it in 1647 as a doctrinal standard.
nodes.why: Presbyterian churches share this doctrinal standard. Congregationalists and Baptists later adapted it for their own confessions.
facts: Parliament convened the assembly in 1643.
The confession teaches two sacraments.
It supports baptism of believers' children.
It teaches spiritual reception of Christ in the Lord's Supper.

nodes.name: Quaker
nodes.summary: George Fox and other English dissenters formed the Religious Society of Friends, emphasizing direct guidance by Christ's Spirit and rejecting required outward rituals.
nodes.why: Friends traditionally understand baptism and Communion as inward experiences of the Spirit, without administering outward sacraments.
facts: The name Quaker arose during Fox's Derby imprisonment in 1650.
Margaret Fell helped organize and sustain the movement.
Friends developed a witness against war and compulsory oaths.
Modern Friends include evangelical, conservative, and liberal communities.
nodes.sacraments: Traditionally no outward sacraments. Baptism and Communion are inward experiences of the Spirit. Some evangelical Friends use outward rites.
nodes.today: Over 400,000 worldwide, especially Kenya, Bolivia, the United States, and Britain.
nodes.disputed: The Anglican link records the English religious setting rather than one formal secession. Some modern liberal Friends do not affirm Nicene Christianity.

nodes.name: Old Believers Schism
nodes.summary: Moscow councils upheld liturgical changes associated with Patriarch Nikon and condemned opponents, deepening separation between Russia's established church and Old Believers.
nodes.why: Disagreements over inherited worship and church authority divided Orthodox Christians as well as Western churches.
facts: Nikon began changing Russian liturgical practices in 1653.
Changes included using three fingers rather than two when crossing oneself.
The councils also deposed Nikon while retaining his reforms.
Authorities persecuted opponents, including Archpriest Avvakum.
nodes.disputed: Reformers sought agreement with Greek practice. Old Believers regarded the inherited Russian rites as the faithful tradition.

nodes.name: Old Believers
nodes.summary: Russian Christians preserved pre-reform worship after the seventeenth-century schism. Their communities divided into groups with priests and groups without priests.
nodes.why: Old Believers share Orthodox beliefs but differ over church authority. Communities without priests cannot celebrate the Eucharist.
facts: Old Believers retained the two-fingered sign of the cross.
Priestly and priestless communities developed different church structures.
The Russian Orthodox Church lifted the old condemnations in 1971.
nodes.sacraments: Priestly groups retain seven mysteries, infant baptism, and Christ's real Eucharistic presence. Priestless groups retain baptism but lack priestly Eucharist and other priest-dependent rites.
nodes.today: Estimated two million in Russia, eastern Europe, and diaspora communities.

nodes.name: Pietism and Spener
nodes.summary: Philipp Jakob Spener published Pia Desideria, urging Bible study, active lay participation, practical Christian living, and better pastoral formation.
nodes.why: Pietism encouraged personal renewal within Protestant churches and influenced Moravians, Methodists, and later revivals.
facts: Spener worked as a Lutheran pastor in Frankfurt.
Small gatherings studied Scripture and encouraged Christian living.
Pietism emphasized personal renewal without forming one new denomination.

nodes.name: Herrnhut Renewal
nodes.summary: Members of Herrnhut's divided refugee community experienced reconciliation and spiritual renewal during a Communion service on August 13, 1727.
nodes.why: A Communion service helped reconcile Herrnhut's divided community, which sustained prayer and sent missionaries abroad.
facts: Count Zinzendorf supported the community on his Saxon estate.
The service took place at nearby Berthelsdorf's Lutheran parish church.
Moravians remember the day as their spiritual birthday.

nodes.name: Methodist
nodes.summary: John and Charles Wesley organized renewal within Anglicanism through disciplined devotion, preaching, and societies. Methodist churches later gained separate ministries and sacramental authority.
nodes.why: Methodists grew from Anglican renewal into separate churches that emphasize grace, conversion, and holy living.
facts: The Oxford Holy Club began in 1729.
John Wesley experienced assurance at Aldersgate in 1738.
Charles Wesley wrote hymns for worship and teaching.
American Methodists formed an independent church in 1784. English separation developed through 1795.
nodes.sacraments: Two sacraments: baptism, including infants, and Holy Communion. Both are means of grace. Methodists affirm Christ's real spiritual presence without transubstantiation.
nodes.today: Over 80 million in World Methodist Council churches, including united churches.
nodes.disputed: 1729 dates the renewal movement. Separate churches emerged later. Wesley resisted treating English Methodism as a new denomination.

nodes.name: First Great Awakening
nodes.summary: Revivals spread through British North America during the 1730s and 1740s. Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield preached conversion and renewed Christian commitment.
nodes.why: Revival preachers spread evangelical emphasis on personal conversion across existing Protestant churches.
facts: Edwards led revival preaching in Northampton, Massachusetts.
Whitefield's preaching tours linked churches across the colonies.
Revivals divided supporters and critics within established churches.
Presbyterians and Baptists also took part and gained converts.
nodes.disputed: Dates approximate the revival period. The Congregationalist link reflects Edwards, but the movement crossed several Protestant branches.

nodes.name: Wesley at Aldersgate
nodes.summary: On May 24, 1738, John Wesley attended a London religious meeting and experienced assurance that Christ had saved him.
nodes.why: Wesley's experience of assurance became central to Methodist teaching while he remained an Anglican priest.
facts: Wesley described his heart as "strangely warmed."
The meeting heard Luther's preface to Romans.
Moravian contacts influenced Wesley's search for assurance.
Wesley continued to identify as an Anglican.

nodes.name: Methodist Separation
nodes.summary: American Methodists organized an independent church in 1784. England's 1795 Plan of Pacification permitted Methodist sacramental ministry, consolidating a gradual break from Anglicanism.
nodes.why: Authority to ordain ministers and administer sacraments helped Methodist societies become separate churches.
facts: The Christmas Conference organized the Methodist Episcopal Church in Baltimore.
Thomas Coke and Francis Asbury led the American church.
England's Plan allowed local societies to approve Methodist Communion services.
nodes.sacraments: The dispute concerned authority to ordain ministers and administer baptism and Communion. Methodists retained the two gospel sacraments.
nodes.disputed: England's separation unfolded gradually. In 1795, Methodist societies gained greater sacramental authority, but no single date defines the break.

nodes.name: US Episcopal Church
nodes.summary: American Anglicans adopted the Episcopal Church's constitution and prayer book in 1789, organizing national church life after the American Revolution.
nodes.why: American Anglicans established their own church government while retaining Anglican worship and sacramental teaching.
facts: The church retained bishops and Anglican worship.
Samuel Seabury became its first bishop in 1784 through Scottish consecration.
William White helped shape representative national governance.
The constitution and General Convention joined bishops, clergy, and lay representatives.
